pages.html:
Optima Academy Online · Discovering Computer Science

A Letter of Welcome 🦉

To our explorer-scholars and the families who travel with them.

Dear Students and Families,

Welcome to Discovering Computer Science. I'm [Instructor name], and I'll be your guide this year as we take on a single, surprisingly large question: what is computer science, and why is it worth learning even if you never write code for a living?

Our answer is that computing is a liberal art — a lens for interpreting the world, as worth studying as literature or logic. So we'll treat this year as an expedition. Each unit charts a new territory on the map of computing: the machine, the network, the logic of programs, algorithms and data, the command line, the programmer's craft, security, and finally intelligence and citizenship in a digital age. In every territory we do three things — build something with our hands, read a foundational text by the people who invented the field (Lovelace, Turing, Berners-Lee, and others), and argue about what it means.

What to expect

  • Self-paced, mastery-based. There's a suggested weekly pace, but students move forward when they've shown they understand — not when the clock says so. Checkpoints can be retaken; they exist for learning, not for gotchas.
  • Online, and social anyway. No live attendance is required, but this is not a solo course. Students post and respond in our discussion board, give real feedback on each other's work, and keep a logbook of reflections. Their writing is their presence here, and it counts toward their grade.
  • Real tools, no special equipment. A computer and a modern web browser are all that's needed. Programming happens in free, browser-based environments; circuits and devices are explored through simulators. A VR headset is optional enrichment — never required, and nothing is hidden behind it.
  • Honest work, including with AI. AI tools may be used to explain, unstick, and check reasoning — then students write and code it themselves, disclose the help, and stand ready to explain their work. We treat this as a skill to learn, not a temptation to police.

How families can help

  • Help your student protect a steady weekly rhythm. Self-paced courses reward routine and punish drift more than any other kind.
  • Ask them what they're building, and ask them to explain it to you. Explaining is the fastest way to find out what you actually understand.
  • Let the struggle happen. A stuck program is not a failure — it's the assignment. Encourage them to post the question rather than abandon the problem.
Access and accommodations. Every activity is self-paced with no time limit, readings are provided as text, and videos are captioned. If your student has an IEP or 504 plan, or needs an alternative format, message me at the start of the course — supports are arranged confidentially.

Reaching me

Message me anytime in Canvas or email [instructor email]; I reply [response time]. There are optional office hours each quarter, and questions are always welcome in the discussion board — often another student has the same one.

One last thing about how I teach. I'm a lead learner, not an oracle. Computing changes faster than any of us can keep up with, and I will happily say "I don't know" in front of a class — right before we go find out. That posture is the course.

I'm glad you're here. Let's go draw the map.

Warmly,
[Instructor name]
Discovering Computer Science · Optima Academy Online

pages.title: Course Syllabus
pages.html:
Optima Academy Online · Florida Course #0200384

Discovering Computer Science

🦉 An expedition into the liberal art of computing.
Course Discovering Computer Science (#0200384) · Year-long elective · Grades 9–12 · Level 2
Format Fully online · self-paced / asynchronous · VR-capable (VR optional, never required)
Instructor [Instructor name] · [instructor email]
Async help Message me in Canvas; I respond [response time]. Optional office hours & live VR experiences each quarter.

Course Description

Discovering Computer Science introduces you to the fundamental principles of computer science, emphasizing its role as a tool for problem-solving, communication, and personal expression. We explore the visible, impactful aspects of computing — how it shapes the world around us — through the design process, data that solves real problems, and the input/output of physical computing (here, via simulators). Through hands-on projects and real-world applications you build the skills to interpret and influence the digital world, whether or not you pursue a career in technology.

Computer science as a liberal art. Computing is fundamental to understanding and participating in modern society, so it is worth learning as part of a liberal education — a critical lens for interpreting the world. In this course we travel that idea as an expedition: each unit is a new territory on the map of computing, charted through a foundational reading, a hands-on activity, and shared inquiry. You are an explorer-scholar, and I am your lead learner — my mantra is, "I may not know every answer, but together we can figure it out."

How This Self-Paced Course Works

  • Suggested pace: a recommended weekly plan keeps you on track to finish in the school year, but you advance when you have demonstrated mastery — not by the clock.
  • Waypoints (mastery checkpoints): short auto-graded checks gate each leg of the journey. Retake them until you reach mastery; they are for learning, not gotchas.
  • Learning is social — asynchronously. You will post and respond in the Agora (discussion boards), give and receive structured feedback in the Council (peer review), keep a Logbook of written/recorded reflections, and publish shared artifacts. No live attendance is required.
  • Getting help: message me anytime in Canvas (I reply [response time]); post questions in the Agora; join optional quarterly office hours or live VR experiences.

The Expedition: Units & Primary Sources

Unit (Territory) Strand focus Primary-source anchor
0 · Base Camp — the Computational CommonsCommunication & collaboration; integrity & responsible AIWing, "Computational Thinking" (2006)
1 · The Machine — hardware & originsComputing systems; I/O (simulators)Moore, "Cramming More Components" (1965)
2 · The Network — connection & the InternetNetworks; the InternetBerners-Lee, "Information Management" (1989)
3 · The Logic of Programs — the explorer's languageProgramming foundations (Code.org / p5.js)Lovelace, Note G (1843)
4 · Algorithms, Data & IntelligenceAlgorithms; data; modeling; intro MLDijkstra, "Go To Considered Harmful" (1968)
5 · Command of the Machine — the command-line frontierProgramming (shell); systems in practiceKernighan & Pike, Unix Programming Environment
6 · The Programmer's Craft — scripting & building togetherScripting; software engineering; collaboration; licensesACM Code of Ethics + open-source licenses
7 · Guarding the Republic — security & cryptographyCybersecurity; cryptography; online safetyKerckhoffs' principle + breach case study
8 · Intelligence & the Digital Citizen — draw your own map (capstone)AI & emerging tech; society, ethics & well-beingTuring, "Computing Machinery & Intelligence" (1950)

Suggested pacing: Units 0–4 in Semester 1; Units 5–8 in Semester 2. Programming runs all year — visual & creative coding (Code.org App Lab, p5.js) in Semester 1, then the command-line and scripting arc as core work in Semester 2.

Standards Alignment

This course is built to Florida's B.E.S.T. Standards for Computer Science (effective July 2024) for course #0200384, and intentionally embeds Florida's Computational Thinking & Reasoning (CTR), Mathematical Thinking & Reasoning (MTR), ELA Expectations (EE), and English Language Development (ELD) standards.

The seven CS strands (SC.912.*) covered:

  • CC — Communication & Collaboration
  • CO — Computing Systems / Organization
  • CS — Cybersecurity
  • ET — Emerging Technologies
  • HS — Health, Safety & Digital Citizenship
  • PE — Programming
  • TI — Technology & Information (impact, ethics, law)

Embedded throughout: SC.K12.CTR.*, MA.K12.MTR.*, ELA.K12.EE.*, and ELD.K12.ELL.SI.1.

Materials & Technology

  • Canvas — your home base for all lessons, discussions, and assessments.
  • Code.org CS Discoveries (App Lab / Game Lab) and the p5.js web editor / Trinket — programming environments.
  • MakeCode micro:bit and Tinkercad Circuits simulators — physical-computing concepts (input/output, circuits). No hardware required; simulators cover the I/O concepts in the standards.
  • Interactive activities hosted by the course on the web and embedded in Canvas (concept explorations, algorithm visualizations, a safe command-line sandbox, cipher tools).
  • A modern web browser (Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari). A VR headset is optional for enrichment experiences only.

Grading & Progress

Progress, not seat-time. Your grade reflects what you produce and how you contribute — milestones reached, artifacts created, and the quality of your participation in the Agora and the Council — not hours logged.

CategoryWeight*What it includes
Projects & Waypoint artifacts40%Rubric-graded unit projects + the capstone ("Draw Your Own Map").
Discussions & peer review (Agora & Council)25%Required. Post-and-respond threads + structured async peer review (you are graded on the feedback you give, too).
Mastery checks (Waypoints)20%Auto-graded formative quizzes; retakes encouraged until mastery.
Logbook reflections15%Written or recorded reflections connecting readings, code, and ideas.

*Provisional weights — confirm against OAO grading policy before publishing.

Academic Integrity & Responsible Use of AI

Your work must be your own. Plagiarism, misrepresenting others' digital work as yours, falsifying data, and uncited copying are violations of academic integrity.

Using AI responsibly. AI tools (chatbots, code assistants) can support your learning — like a tutor or a reference — but they do not replace your thinking, and they are not always right. In this course:

  • Use AI to explain concepts, get unstuck, or check your reasoning — then write/code it yourself and be ready to explain it.
  • Disclose when and how you used an AI tool on a graded artifact (a one-line note is fine).
  • Never submit AI output as your own original work, and never paste confidential or personal data into AI tools.
  • On peer review and collaborative projects, irresponsible AI use (e.g., fabricated feedback or data) undermines your teammates and violates TI.2.6.

This section will be reconciled with Optima Classical Academy's official academic-integrity and AI-use policy language before publishing.

Accommodations

Optima Academy Online provides accommodations for students with disabilities as identified in an Individual Educational Plan (IEP) or Section 504 plan, consistent with federal and Florida law. Accommodations may include adjusted time demands and schedules, alternative instructional materials and formats, assistive technology, and modified assignments or assessments. Please share your plan with me at the start of the course so supports can be arranged; documentation is kept confidential. This course is built to WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards, and its self-paced design supports extended time by default.

Our Asynchronous Community Norms

  • Be present in writing. Since we rarely meet live, your posts and feedback are your presence here. Contribute generously.
  • Cite your evidence and use a respectful, scholarly voice in the Agora and the Council.
  • Treat errors as discoveries. Bugs and wrong turns are how explorers learn — share them.
  • Respond, don't just post. Read peers' work, build on their ideas, and disagree kindly with reasons.
  • Reach out early. If you're stuck or falling behind the suggested pace, message me — that's what a lead learner is for.

pages.html:
Unit 5 · Territory Five · Semester 2 Begins

Command of the Machine: The Command-Line Frontier ⌨️

Welcome back, explorer. Semester 1 taught you how machines, networks, and programs work. Semester 2 begins by dropping the pictures: no icons, no buttons — just you, a blinking cursor, and the most powerful interface ever built. This is how professionals talk to computers.

Your route through this territory

  1. 5.01 — What Is a Shell?
    Why the terminal never died — and the 1974 paper that started it all.
  2. 5.02 — Navigating the Filesystem
    pwd, ls, cd — learning to move without a mouse. Missions 1–3.
  3. 5.03 — Making & Moving Files
    Create, write, copy, move, delete — from the keyboard. Missions 4–6.
  4. 5.04 — Power Tools: Pipes & grep
    Search hundreds of files in one line by snapping small tools together. Missions 7–9.
  5. 5.05 — Permissions & the Vault
    Who may read, who may write — and cracking the locked file. Mission 10.
  6. Waypoint 5 + the Needle in the Haystack investigation.

What you'll be able to do

  • Navigate and manage a filesystem entirely from the keyboard.
  • Compose small commands into powerful one-liners with pipes.
  • Search at scale with grep — a thousand files as easily as one.
  • Read and change file permissions, and explain why they exist.

Your training ground

Everything happens in the Shell Sandbox — a simulated terminal with a virtual expedition filesystem, embedded right in your lessons. It looks and behaves like the real thing, but it's completely safe: nothing you type can touch your actual computer. Ten auto-checked missions guide you from your first pwd to cracking a permissions-locked vault.

Heads up: the sandbox resets if you reload the page — that's by design (real shells forget nothing; simulations forgive everything). Finish a lesson's missions in one sitting, or enjoy the re-run: repetition is exactly how command-line fluency is built.
Accommodations & access. The shell is 100% keyboard-driven by nature, with all output announced to screen readers as text. No time limits; missions can be retried endlessly. Need an alternative format or have an IEP/504 plan? Message your instructor — supports are arranged confidentially.

Ready? Meet the shell in 5.01 →

pages.title: 5.01 What Is a Shell?
pages.html:
Unit 5 · Lesson 5.01

What Is a Shell?

I can…
  • explain what a shell is and how it relates to the operating system;
  • weigh when a command line beats a graphical interface — and when it doesn't;
  • describe the 1974 design ideas that still run most of the world's computers.

🧭 The interface that refused to die

Fifty years of touchscreens, windows, and voice assistants — and yet every serious server, every cloud datacenter, every developer's laptop still runs a black window with a blinking cursor. Why? Because the command line is not a relic. It's the power-user interface: precise, scriptable, and fast in ways a mouse can never be.

The shell's place in the machine

Remember Unit 1's chain: Application → Operating System → Driver → Hardware. A shell is a special application whose whole job is to be your voice to the operating system. You type a command; the shell interprets it and asks the OS to do it; the OS commands the hardware. It's called a "shell" because it wraps around the OS kernel — the layer you touch.

Graphical interface (GUI)Command line (shell)
Discoverable — you can see what's possible.Memorized — you must know what to say.
Great for one thing at a time.Great for hundreds of things at a time ("rename 500 files" is one line).
Actions vanish when done.Commands are text — repeatable, shareable, and (next unit) scriptable.
Needs a screen and pointer.Works over the tiniest connection — how admins fix servers an ocean away.

Neither wins everywhere. Choosing the right interface for the task is the same tool-evaluation skill you've been sharpening since Unit 1.

📜 Primary source: the paper behind the prompt (1974)

Dennis M. Ritchie & Ken Thompson, "The UNIX Time-Sharing System." Communications of the ACM, Vol. 17, No. 7 (July 1974). The operating system described here is the direct ancestor of Linux, macOS, and Android — and the shell you're about to use is its child.

📄 Read the paper (PDF, UC Berkeley) →

Access: this recreated edition has selectable text (screen-reader/text-to-speech friendly). Required reading: the introduction and Section 6 ("The Shell") — the excerpts below carry the key ideas.

The passages that matter most

"It is hoped… the users of UNIX will find that the most important characteristics of the system are its simplicity, elegance, and ease of use."

"Perhaps the most important achievement of UNIX is to demonstrate that a powerful operating system for interactive use need not be expensive either in equipment or in human effort…"

"A sequence of commands separated by vertical bars causes the Shell to execute all the commands simultaneously and to arrange that the standard output of each command be delivered to the standard input of the next command in the sequence." (Section 6.2, "Filters" — this is the pipe, and you'll wield it in 5.04.)

In plain language: two researchers at Bell Labs built, in under two person-years, an operating system whose bet was simplicity — many small tools, each doing one thing well, connected by pipes so their powers combine. The bet paid off so completely that their design runs most of the world's computers today, and the philosophy — "do one thing well, then compose" — became a design creed far beyond software.

Read with these questions (for the Agora)

  1. What did Ritchie & Thompson hope users would find most important about UNIX? (Quote it.)
  2. The pipe lets small programs combine into big solutions. Where else do you see "small pieces, freely combined" beat "one giant do-everything thing"? (LEGO? A kitchen? An orchestra?)
  3. Modern apps mostly hide the command line from you. What's gained by that — and what's lost?

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to "Do One Thing Well." Post your take (with a quoted line from the paper), then reply to two classmates.

Accommodations & access. The excerpts above carry the required ideas; the PDF has real text for read-aloud tools. Respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 5.02 Navigating the Filesystem
pages.html:
Unit 5 · Lesson 5.02

Navigating the Filesystem

I can…
  • always know where I am in a filesystem (pwd) and what's here (ls);
  • move anywhere with cd, using absolute and relative paths;
  • read files from the command line with cat.

🧭 The filesystem is a tree — and you're standing in it

Every file lives somewhere in one big upside-down tree that starts at the root, written /. Folders (directories) branch; files are the leaves. In a GUI you look at the tree from outside. In a shell you stand inside it — you are always at some location, and three commands are your senses:

CommandMeansThink of it as
pwdprint working directory"Where am I?"
lslist"What's here?"
cdchange directory"Walk there."

Two ways to write an address

  • Absolute path — the full route from the root: /home/scholar/field-notes. Works from anywhere, like a full street address.
  • Relative path — from where you're standing: field-notes (a folder here), or .. ("the folder above me"). Shorter, like saying "next door."

And to read a file where you stand: cat FILE prints its contents. That's command-line input (your typed command) and output (the text that comes back) — the same loop as ever, in its purest form.

🛠️ Missions 1–3: get your bearings

Open the Shell Sandbox and complete the first three missions: find where you are, explore the field notes, and read what the locals told the expedition. Type hint anytime.

Open in a new tab if needed: Shell Sandbox ↗ · The sandbox resets on reload — finishing a lesson's missions in one sitting is ideal, and re-runs build speed.

Accommodations & access. The shell is keyboard-native; output is plain text announced to screen readers; missions retry endlessly with no timer. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 5.03 Making & Moving Files
pages.html:
Unit 5 · Lesson 5.03

Making & Moving Files

I can…
  • create directories and files from the command line;
  • send a command's output into a file with redirection (> and >>);
  • copy, move, and delete files — carefully.

🧭 From explorer to builder

Yesterday you could only look and walk. Today you reshape the terrain. Five builders and one superpower:

CommandDoesWatch out
mkdir NAMEMake a directoryFails politely if it already exists.
touch NAMEMake an empty file—
cp SRC DESTCopy (original stays)Overwrites DEST silently if it exists.
mv SRC DESTMove or rename (original goes)Same silent-overwrite habit.
rm NAMEDeleteNo trash can. No undo. The shell assumes you mean it.

The superpower: redirection

Any command's output can be captured into a file instead of printed:

echo "Day 4: reached the river" >> log.txt   # APPEND to the end of log.txt
echo "Fresh start"              >  log.txt   # OVERWRITE log.txt entirely

One arrow > replaces; two arrows >> add to the end. Mixing them up is the classic way to vaporize a file — say it out loud before you press Enter. (Professionals do.)

🛠️ Missions 4–6: build your basecamp

Back in the Shell Sandbox ↗ (or the copy embedded in 5.02): make a basecamp directory, write your first log entry into it with >>, and copy the expedition map in. Verify each step with ls and cat — command, then check, every time. (Doing missions 1–6 in one sitting? Even better — the re-run of 1–3 is free practice.)

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

rm has no undo, and > overwrites without asking. The shell trusts you completely. Is that good design? When is an interface right to assume you mean what you say?

Accommodations & access. Keyboard-native; no timers; endless retries (the sandbox forgives everything — that's what it's for). Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 5.04 Power Tools: Pipes & grep
pages.html:
Unit 5 · Lesson 5.04

Power Tools: Pipes & grep

I can…
  • search inside files — even hundreds at once — with grep;
  • measure text with wc, and sample it with head and tail;
  • chain small tools into one powerful command with the pipe.

🧭 The promise from 1974, kept

In 5.01 you read Ritchie & Thompson describing commands "separated by vertical bars," each one's output flowing into the next. Today that sentence becomes muscle memory. Three small tools first:

ToolOne job, done wellExample
grep WORD FILESPrint only the lines containing WORD (-i = ignore case; * = all files here)grep AURUM *
wc -l FILECount lineswc -l supplies.txt
head / tail FILEShow just the first / last linestail log-007.txt

Then the pipe: |

grep -i gold * | wc -l
#   └── step 1: find every line mentioning gold, in every file here
#                └── step 2: count those lines
# Two small tools; one question answered: "how often do the records mention gold?"

The pipe | pours the output of the left command into the input of the right one. Neither tool knows about the other; neither was designed for this exact question — and that's the genius. Small tools, freely combined, answer questions their authors never imagined. This is decomposition running in reverse: instead of breaking a problem down, you snap solutions together.

And here's your Unit 2 + Unit 4 payoff: this is search at scale. A newsroom greps a million leaked documents; a sysadmin greps a year of server logs; a biologist greps a genome. Same tool you're about to use on twelve expedition records.

🛠️ Missions 7–9: the hunt begins

In the Shell Sandbox ↗: count the supply lines, then hunt the word AURUM through the expedition records with grep, then chain your first pipe to count the gold mentions. These three missions are the heart of the unit project.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Compare finding AURUM by hand (open all 12 files, read every line) versus grep AURUM *. Now imagine 12,000 files. At what point does the tool stop being a convenience and become the only possible way?

Accommodations & access. Keyboard-native; output is plain text; hints available every mission; no timers. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

Next: 5.05 — Permissions & the Vault →

pages.title: 5.05 Permissions & the Vault
pages.html:
Unit 5 · Lesson 5.05

Permissions & the Vault

I can…
  • read a file's permissions with ls -l;
  • change what's allowed with chmod;
  • explain why operating systems enforce who-may-do-what.

🧭 The OS is a doorkeeper

Try to read the treasure file and the shell snaps back: Permission denied. Who denied you? Not the file — files are just data. The operating system did: every time any program touches any file, the OS checks the file's permissions first. That's the OS-as-manager idea from Unit 1, caught in the act.

Reading the lock: ls -l

$ ls -l
-rw-     126  day2.txt        # r = readable, w = writable
--w-     126  treasure.txt    # no r: reading DENIED (writing still allowed)
drwx       -  field-notes/    # d = it's a directory

That little string of letters is the lock. r = may read, w = may write, and on real systems x = may run as a program, with separate settings for the owner, their group, and everyone else. Our sandbox keeps it simple — read and write — but the idea is identical.

Changing the lock: chmod

chmod +r treasure.txt    # grant read
chmod -w treasure.txt    # revoke write

chmod ("change mode") edits the permissions — if you have the right to. Why does any of this exist? Because computers are shared: your files against other users' mistakes, system files against your mistakes, and everything against malicious programs. Permissions are the first wall of computer security — in Unit 7 you'll see what happens when walls like this fail, and meet the "super-user" who can bypass them all.

🛠️ Mission 10: crack the vault

In the Shell Sandbox ↗: the file /expedition/locked/treasure.txt refuses to open. Inspect it with ls -l, grant yourself read access, and claim the expedition seal. You'll need the seal code for your project report.

✍️ Then: the unit project

Open "Needle in the Haystack" — your full shell investigation, start to finish, with a short report. It's the capstone of this territory.

Accommodations & access. Keyboard-native; hints on demand; no timers; endless retries. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

Finish the territory: Needle in the Haystack + Waypoint 5. Next: Unit 6 — where commands become scripts, and you build software together. 🧭

pages.title: 6.00 Welcome to The Programmer's Craft
pages.html:
Unit 6 · Territory Six

The Programmer's Craft: Scripting & Building Together 🛠️

Last territory you commanded the machine one line at a time. Now your commands become programs — and, for the first time, you won't build alone. Real software is a team craft: planned, reviewed, documented, and owned. Welcome to the guild.

Your route through this territory

  1. 6.01 — From Commands to Scripts
    Variables and read: your shell commands become reusable programs. Script Lab challenges 1–2.
  2. 6.02 — Scripts That Decide & Repeat
    if/elif/else and loops — Unit 3's logic, reborn at the command line. Challenges 3–5.
  3. 6.03 — Building to a Plan
    The software development cycle: design first, then build, then test. Clean code and comments.
  4. 6.04 — The Council
    The craft's oldest tradition: reviewing each other's work. You'll learn to give feedback that makes code better.
  5. 6.05 — Who Owns Code?
    The ACM Code of Ethics, and the licenses that let strangers build together.
  6. Waypoint 6 + the team project: The Toolmaker's Guild.

What you'll be able to do

  • Write shell scripts with variables, input, decisions, and loops.
  • Plan a program before building it — and build to the plan.
  • Review a peer's code for readability and usability, and revise from the reviews you receive.
  • Choose and apply a software license, and explain who may use, change, and share your work.

The big project — and the Council

The Toolmaker's Guild: in a small async team, you'll design, build, review, license, and publish a shell-script tool — with a design doc, a contribution log, and two rounds of structured peer review in the Council. Everything is asynchronous: you never need to meet live. Your posts, reviews, and commits are the collaboration.

Accommodations & access. Self-paced; the Script Lab is keyboard-native with no timers and endless retries; team roles are flexible (writer, tester, documenter, reviewer are all real contributions). Reviews and reflections may be typed or recorded. IEP/504 supports arranged confidentially — message your instructor.

Ready? Write your first script in 6.01 →

pages.title: 6.01 From Commands to Scripts
pages.html:
Unit 6 · Lesson 6.01

From Commands to Scripts

I can…
  • explain what makes a script different from a typed command;
  • store values in variables and use them with $;
  • make a script interactive with read.

🧭 Commands that outlive the moment

Every command you typed in Unit 5 vanished the instant it finished. But remember the promise of the command line: commands are text. Put them in a file, and that file becomes a script — a program the shell can run again and again. A script is just your Unit 5 fluency, saved. And the moment commands become programs, everything from Unit 3 comes flooding back: variables, input, decisions, loops.

The two new moves

# a comment — the shell ignores it; humans thank you (more in 6.03)
EXPEDITION=Aurora            # a VARIABLE: a name for a value (no spaces around =)
echo "Onward, $EXPEDITION!"  # $ fetches the value  →  Onward, Aurora!

echo "What is your name?"
read NAME                    # read pauses and stores what the user types
echo "Welcome, $NAME!"       # a script that LISTENS — input → process → output
  • Variables work like Unit 3's, with shell spelling: NAME=value to set (no spaces around =), $NAME to use.
  • read is the shell's prompt() — and your Unit 3 prompt-writing craft applies unchanged: tell the user exactly what to type.
  • Arithmetic: N=$((N + 1)) computes inside $(( )).

🛠️ Script Lab: challenges 1–2

The Script Lab below is a safe, simulated script runner — write in the editor, feed it pretend user input, run, and check. Complete 1 · Name it and 2 · Greeter.

Open in a new tab if needed: Script Lab ↗ · Progress resets on reload — finish a lesson's challenges in one sitting.

Accommodations & access. Keyboard-native; no timers; endless retries; every concept restated in text above the lab. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

Next: 6.02 — Scripts That Decide & Repeat →

pages.title: 6.02 Scripts That Decide & Repeat
pages.html:
Unit 6 · Lesson 6.02

Scripts That Decide & Repeat

I can…
  • write selection in a script: if / elif / else;
  • write iteration: for over a list, while over a condition;
  • combine them into a validation loop that guards a script's input.

🧭 Old friends, new spelling

You already own these ideas — selection and iteration from Unit 3, the algorithm building blocks from Unit 4. Only the costume changes. The shell writes its Boolean questions in square brackets, and closes its blocks with words instead of braces:

read AGE
if [ $AGE -ge 13 ]; then          # -ge means >=   (also: -gt -lt -le -eq -ne, = and != for words)
  echo "Welcome aboard"
elif [ $AGE -ge 10 ]; then
  echo "Almost — bring a guardian"
else
  echo "Come back later"
fi                                 # 'if' spelled backwards closes the block

for DAY in Mon Tue Wed; do         # FOR: walk a list
  echo "March on $DAY"
done

N=5
while [ $N -gt 0 ]; do             # WHILE: repeat while true
  echo $N
  N=$((N - 1))                     # the loop must change its own variable...
done                               # ...or it never ends
echo "Liftoff!"

The move that makes tools trustworthy

Put while + if together and you get the same validation loop you built in Unit 3 — the guard that makes a script safe to hand to a stranger:

read DAYS
while [ $DAYS -lt 1 ]; do
  echo "Days must be at least 1 — try again:"
  read DAYS
done
echo "Packing rations for $DAYS days."

Your team's tool in this unit's project must guard its input like this — a tool that crashes on bad input fails the person using it.

🛠️ Script Lab: challenges 3–5

Back to the Script Lab ↗ (or the copy embedded in 6.01): complete 3 · Gatekeeper, 4 · The March, and 5 · Countdown. Watch challenge 3's edge case — the checker tests age 13 exactly. Then submit the assignment "Script Lab Log".

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

You've now written selection and iteration in two different languages (JavaScript in Unit 3, shell here). What stayed exactly the same? What was just spelling?

pages.title: 6.03 Building to a Plan
pages.html:
Unit 6 · Lesson 6.03

Building to a Plan

I can…
  • walk the software development cycle: plan → design → build → test → improve;
  • write a design doc before writing code — requirements, structure, tests, time;
  • write comments that help the next person (who is often future-you).

🧭 Amateurs start typing; professionals start planning

Your Script Lab challenges were small enough to improvise. Real software isn't — and team software never is: your teammates can't build against a plan that lives only in your head. That's why the craft has a cycle:

PLAN → DESIGN → BUILD → TEST → IMPROVE ↻

It's a loop, not a line — testing sends you back to improve, and improving may reopen the design. You've lived this cycle in miniature (First Sketch, the Interactive Machine, Model the World); this unit makes it explicit and shared.

The design doc: a program on paper first

Before your team writes a line of the project tool, you'll write its design doc — four short sections:

SectionAnswers
RequirementsWhat must the tool do? For whom? What inputs, what outputs, what must never happen (crash on bad input)?
Structural designThe pieces and their order — decompose the tool into named chunks (greet → gather input → validate → compute → report), each small enough for one person to own.
Test planThe inputs you'll try before calling it done — including at least one designed to break it.
Time estimatesWho does which chunk, by when. Estimates will be wrong — writing them down is how teams find out early.

Clean code: comments are for teammates

When several people build one program, the code itself must communicate. Two habits carry most of the weight:

# ration-calc.sh — computes daily rations for an expedition
# team: Ada (input+validation), Grace (calculation), Alan (output+tests)

read CREW          # how many people are marching
read DAYS          # trip length in days

# 3 meals per person per day, plus 10% spare — agreed in design doc
MEALS=$((CREW * DAYS * 3))
  • Name things honestly. MEALS beats M. A good name is a comment that can't go stale.
  • Comment the why, not the what. "plus 10% spare — agreed in design doc" explains a decision; "adds ten percent" just repeats the code. A header comment saying what the file is and who owns which part turns a script into a team artifact.

This is Dijkstra's clarity argument (Unit 4) grown up: on a team, unreadable code isn't a style problem — it's a broken promise to your collaborators.

✍️ Do this: start the Guild project

Open "The Toolmaker's Guild" and complete Phase 1: form your team thread, choose a tool idea, and write the design doc together — asynchronously, in the project discussion space. Build only after the plan exists. (That ordering is graded.)

Accommodations & access. Design docs may be written, drawn, or recorded; team roles are flexible and all count as contribution. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 6.04 The Council
pages.html:
Unit 6 · Lesson 6.04

The Council: Reviewing Each Other's Work ⚖️

I can…
  • review a program for functionality, readability, usability, and style;
  • give feedback that is specific, kind, and actionable — and revise from feedback I receive;
  • explain how review changes what gets built.

🧭 No code ships unreviewed

At every serious software company on Earth, code written by one person is read by another before it ships. Not because programmers distrust each other — because review works: a second pair of eyes catches what the author has gone blind to, and explaining your choices makes them better. In our expedition, this tradition is the Council, and it runs entirely asynchronously.

The four lenses of a review

LensAskHow to check
FunctionalityDoes it do what the design doc promised?Run it — including the test plan's break-it input.
ReadabilityCould a stranger follow this code?Honest names? Why-comments? Clear structure?
UsabilityCould a stranger use it?Clear prompts? Survives bad input? Helpful output?
Style & standardsDoes it follow the team's agreed conventions?Consistent naming, header comment, agreed structure.

How to say it: the reviewer's craft

A review is judged by whether it helps. Three rules:

  • Be specific. "Line 12's prompt doesn't say the answer must be a number" beats "prompts could be better."
  • Be actionable. Every criticism comes with a suggested next move.
  • Review the code, not the coder. "This name confused me" — never "you're bad at naming." And say what's good, specifically: authors need to know what to keep.
A review comment worth writing: "Functionality: works for all my test inputs including 0 — nice guard loop. Readability: the header comment told me exactly who owns what. One fix: the variable X on line 9 holds the ration total — naming it TOTAL_MEALS would save the next reader a minute. Usability: the final message doesn't say the units; add 'meals' to the echo."

Receiving reviews has a craft too: assume good intent, ask for clarification instead of defending, and respond to every point — fixed, or why not. Disagreement is fine; silence isn't. (These are the Agora norms from Base Camp, pointed at code.)

✍️ Do this: sit the Council

Open the assignment "The Council: Review Round". You'll review two peers' tools with the four lenses, then revise your own team's tool from the reviews it received — and log what changed. You are graded on the reviews you give, not just the tool you built. That's not a technicality; it's the point: in this craft, making others' work better is part of the work.

Accommodations & access. Reviews may be typed or recorded; the four-lens table doubles as your checklist. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 6.05 Who Owns Code?
pages.html:
Unit 6 · Lesson 6.05

Who Owns Code?

I can…
  • tell open source, freeware, and proprietary licenses apart;
  • explain how a license both shares and protects a creator's work — and why access ≠ permission to distribute;
  • use the ACM Code of Ethics as a professional compass.

🧭 Your team is about to publish. Under what terms?

The Guild tool is nearly done, and the last design decision isn't technical: when you publish it, what may other people do with it? Copy it? Change it? Sell it? Every piece of software you've ever touched answered those questions with a license — and now you will too.

The three families

FamilyYou may…Examples
Open sourceUse, read the code, change it, and share it. Permissive licenses (MIT) ask little more than credit; copyleft licenses (GPL) add a condition: your changed version must stay open too.Linux (GPL), p5.js (LGPL), most tools this course runs on
FreewareUse it free — but the source is closed: no reading, no changing. Free as in price, not freedom.Many free apps and games
ProprietaryOnly what the paid license grants — usually run-it-only, no copying, no redistribution.Windows, Photoshop, most commercial software

For non-code creations (writing, images, music) the same idea lives in Creative Commons licenses — CC BY means "share, with credit."

The trap to remember: being able to access something is not the right to distribute it. You can read a proprietary program's files, screenshot a paywalled article, download a freeware installer — and still have zero permission to re-share any of them. Ownership and access are different things; the license, not the download button, defines your rights.

And notice: a license shares and protects at once. MIT shares maximally while protecting the author's credit; GPL shares while protecting the commons itself (nobody can lock it up); proprietary protects the business that funds the work. Choosing one is choosing what you want your work to do in the world. That's also the difference between legal and ethical: the license is law you wrote — the reasons behind it are ethics.

📜 Primary source: the profession's compass

ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct (Association for Computing Machinery, 2018) — the ethical charter computing professionals worldwide hold themselves to.

📄 Read the Code (full text, acm.org) →

Access: full accessible HTML. Read the Preamble and Section 1 (General Ethical Principles); the excerpts below anchor the discussion.

1.1 — "Contribute to society and to human well-being, acknowledging that all people are stakeholders in computing."

1.5 — "Respect the work required to produce new ideas, inventions, creative works, and computing artifacts."

3.1 — "Ensure that the public good is the central concern during all professional computing work."

Notice what the Code is not: a law. No police enforce 1.1. It's a profession telling its members — and the public — what it stands for. Principle 1.5 is where this lesson's two halves meet: respecting creative work is the ethic; licenses are the legal machinery we built to honor it.

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to "The Public Good." Post your take on the Code (with a quoted principle), then reply to two classmates.

✍️ Then: license and publish

Finish The Toolmaker's Guild: your team chooses a license for the tool (and defends the choice in one paragraph), adds proper credit for anything you drew on (citation tools count here too), and publishes the final tool + design doc to the class showcase for a different audience than yourselves — that's the last phase of the project.

Accommodations & access. The excerpts above anchor the required reading; the full Code is accessible HTML. Respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

Unit 7 · Territory Seven

Guarding the Republic: Security, Cryptography & Safety 🛡️

You've built machines, networks, and programs. Now learn to defend them — and yourself. In this territory you'll think like an attacker to become a better defender, master the mathematics of secrets, and build real strategies to stay safe and stand up for others online.

Your route through this territory

  1. 7.01 — Why Security Matters
    Threats to your data, the difference between viruses and worms, and how to weigh what an attack really costs.
  2. 7.02 — The Human Exploit
    Social engineering: why the easiest system to hack is a person — and how to spot the con.
  3. 7.03 — Locks & Keys
    Cryptography: the principles of keeping secrets, and a 140-year-old rule that still governs it.
  4. 7.04 — Guarding Networks, Devices & Data
    Protecting connections, hardware, and the data that never truly disappears.
  5. 7.05 — Standing Up Online
    Cyberbullying, the courage to report, and strategies that actually help.
  6. Waypoint 7 + the project: The Defender's Dossier.

What you'll be able to do

  • Identify threats to confidentiality and evaluate the real cost of an attack.
  • Trace a social-engineering con and name where it could be stopped.
  • Explain the principles of cryptography — and why the algorithm can be public while only the key is secret.
  • Protect your networks, devices, and personal data — and know how and when to report harm online.

The big project

The Defender's Dossier has two halves: analyze a real recent cyber attack (what happened, who was hurt, what it cost, what would have stopped it), and create a public "defend yourself online" artifact — a guide, poster, or short video that helps real people protect themselves and stand up against online harassment.

A note on this unit: we study attacks in order to defend against them — never to carry them out. Everything here is for protection, and the cryptography tools are educational demonstrations, not for real secrets. Some topics (online predators, cyberbullying) are serious; if anything here brings up something you're dealing with, please talk to your instructor or a trusted adult.
Accommodations & access. Self-paced; interactives are keyboard-operable and screen-reader friendly; the project artifact may be a written guide, poster, slideshow, or recording — your choice. IEP/504 supports arranged confidentially — message your instructor.

pages.title: 7.01 Why Security Matters
pages.html:
Unit 7 · Lesson 7.01

Why Security Matters

I can…
  • identify everyday risks to keeping data confidential;
  • explain the difference between a virus and a worm;
  • evaluate an attack's impact — on people and on economies — not just on machines.

🧭 The three questions of security

Security professionals guard three things, often called the CIA triad: Confidentiality (only the right people can read it), Integrity (it hasn't been secretly changed), and Availability (it's there when you need it). This unit leans hardest on the first — keeping secrets secret — because that's where most everyday risk lives.

Risks to confidentiality hide in plain sight

Not every threat is a hooded hacker. The most common ones are ordinary:

RiskWhat it isSimple defense
Shoulder surfingSomeone reads your screen or watches you type a password.Angle your screen; shield the keypad.
Unlocked / borrowed devicesA phone left unlocked, a shared computer left logged in.Lock screens; log out; short auto-lock timers.
Theft of sensitive itemsA stolen laptop, a lost USB drive, a photographed document.Encryption; don't store secrets you don't need.

Malware: virus vs. worm

Malicious software ("malware") comes in families. Two get confused constantly, and the difference is exactly one thing — does it need a human?

🦠 Virus

Attaches to a file or program and spreads only when a human does something — opens the attachment, runs the program, shares the file. Like a cold: it needs someone to pass it along.

🐛 Worm

Copies itself across a network with no human help at all, hunting for other machines automatically. Like a spreading wildfire — it doesn't wait for anyone.

The distinction matters for defense: a virus is slowed by careful humans ("don't open that attachment"); a worm has to be stopped by the systems — patched software, firewalls, network segmentation — because it never asks permission.

Evaluating an attack: count the human cost

When you assess a real attack (you will, in the project), don't stop at "the computer went down." Weigh the social and economic impact:

  • People: whose private data leaked? Medical records, grades, messages, identities? What can be done to them with it?
  • Money: ransom paid, business lost during downtime, cost to notify and protect victims, fines, lawsuits.
  • Trust: hardest to measure, slowest to rebuild — customers, patients, or students who no longer feel safe.

A breach that "only" leaked a database can wreck thousands of lives and cost millions — often far more than the flashy attacks that make headlines.

The rules of the road: Internet safety policy

You don't defend alone. Schools, districts, and states set Internet safety policies — the rules governing acceptable use, what's monitored, and how to report problems. Florida schools operate under state and district guidelines (and federal rules tied to school internet funding). Knowing your school's policy — where it lives, what it requires, who to contact — is itself a security skill.

Find it: locate your school or district's Acceptable Use Policy / Internet safety policy (your instructor will link it). You'll reference it in the project — and it tells you exactly how to report the harms we cover in 7.05.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Look at the confidentiality risks table. Which one are you most exposed to right now, honestly — and what's one change you could make today?

pages.title: 7.02 The Human Exploit
pages.html:
Unit 7 · Lesson 7.02

The Human Exploit

I can…
  • trace the four stages of a social-engineering attack;
  • recognize dangers of direct online contact and protect my personal information;
  • use privacy settings, cookie controls, and app permissions to shrink my exposure.

🧭 Why hack a computer when you can fool a person?

The strongest password in the world is useless if someone politely asks for it — and gets it. Social engineering is manipulating people into giving up access or information, and it's behind a huge share of real breaches. The good news: it follows a predictable cycle, and once you can name the cycle, you can break it.

🛠️ Explore: trace the con

Follow an attacker through all four stages against a school office. At each step, name the tactic and find where a single verification step would have stopped everything.

Open in a new tab if needed: Trace the Con ↗

The cycle to remember: information gathering → relationship building → exploitation → execution. Every stage has a defense, but the strongest is the simplest — verify through an independent channel, and let urgency be a reason to slow down, never speed up.

When the target is a person, not an office

The same cycle is aimed at individuals — and can turn dangerous. Direct electronic contact (chats, DMs, game voice, "friend" requests) is where predators operate: they gather details from your profile, build false trust over days or weeks, then exploit it — pressuring for personal information, images, money, or a meeting. Human trafficking recruiters use exactly this playbook.

Red flags in direct contact: someone who moves fast to be your "only" friend; asks you to keep the relationship secret; requests photos, your location, or personal/financial details; showers gifts or flattery; or pushes to move onto a private app. If this is happening to you or someone you know, tell a trusted adult — you'll learn exactly how and where to report in 7.05, and it is never the target's fault.

Shrink your attack surface

Attackers start with information gathering — so give them less to gather. Three dials you control:

DialWhat it controlsDo this
Privacy settingsWho can see your posts, profile, location, friend list.Set accounts to private; audit "who can see this" yearly.
CookiesSmall files that track you across sites for ads/profiling.Reject non-essential cookies; clear them; use private windows.
App permissionsWhat an app may access: camera, mic, contacts, location.Grant only what the app truly needs; revoke the rest.

Why does a flashlight app want your contacts and location? It usually doesn't need them — it wants to collect them. Every permission you deny is information an attacker (or a data broker) can't gather.

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to "Spot the Con." Share a real (or realistic) example of a social-engineering attempt — a phishing text, a too-good giveaway, a suspicious DM. Name which stage of the cycle it's in and the red flag that gives it away. Reply to two classmates with the verification step that would defeat their example.

Accommodations & access. The widget is keyboard-operable with all text announced; the tables restate every point. Respond by typing or recording. Sensitive topic — supports and alternatives available confidentially (IEP/504); reach out anytime.

pages.title: 7.03 Locks & Keys
pages.html:
Unit 7 · Lesson 7.03

Locks & Keys: The Principles of Cryptography

I can…
  • explain the five principles cryptography provides;
  • encrypt and decrypt with classic ciphers, and crack a weak one;
  • state Kerckhoffs' principle and why the key — not the algorithm — is the secret.

🧭 The art of the secret

Cryptography is the mathematics of protecting information — the technology under every password box, every "🔒" in your browser, every private message. It scrambles a readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using an algorithm and a key, so only someone with the key can reverse it.

The five things cryptography gives us

PrincipleGuarantees…Everyday example
ConfidentialityOnly the intended reader can read it.Your messages look like gibberish to your carrier.
IntegrityIt wasn't altered in transit.A download that fails its checksum is rejected.
AuthenticationThe sender is who they claim to be.The 🔒 proves you're really on your bank's site.
Non-repudiationThe sender can't later deny they sent it.A digital signature on a contract.
Key managementKeys are generated, shared, stored & retired safely.The hardest part in practice — and where most real failures happen.

Notice the last one. The math of modern encryption is essentially unbreakable — so attackers rarely attack the math. They attack the keys: stolen, guessed, reused, or leaked. Great cryptography with sloppy key management is a bank vault with the combination on a sticky note.

🛠️ Explore: the Cipher Lab

Encrypt a message with the classic Caesar and Vigenère ciphers, then switch to Crack It and brute-force an intercepted Caesar message. Feel why a 25-key cipher is hopeless — and why the fix is a bigger key, not a secret method.

Open in a new tab if needed: Cipher Lab ↗ · These are teaching ciphers, breakable by design — never use them for real secrets.

📜 Primary source: Kerckhoffs' principle (1883)

Auguste Kerckhoffs, "La Cryptographie Militaire." Journal des sciences militaires, 1883. A French linguist laid down six rules for military cryptography — and one of them still governs how the entire field works, 140 years later.

📄 Read the article + English principles (petitcolas.net) →

Access: the page hosts the 1883 original and an accessible English list of all six principles. The second principle — quoted below — is the one to know.

"The system must not require secrecy and can be stolen by the enemy without causing trouble." — Kerckhoffs' 2nd principle (English rendering)

In plain language: assume the enemy knows exactly how your cipher works. A cryptosystem is only trustworthy if it stays secure even when the whole method is public — with the key as the single secret. This flips intuition: hiding your algorithm ("security through obscurity") feels safer but isn't — because secrets leak, and a method whose safety depended on staying hidden collapses the moment it does. The Cipher Lab proved it: knowing it's "a Caesar cipher" didn't help you until you found the key, and a bigger keyspace — not a hidden method — is what makes real ciphers unbreakable. Claude Shannon restated it in 1949 as simply: "the enemy knows the system." It's why the world's strongest encryption algorithms are published openly for everyone to attack — and still hold.

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to "The Enemy Knows the System." Post (with the quoted principle): why would security experts publish their encryption methods for attackers to study? Give one analogy from outside computing (a lock design, a safe rating, a scientific result that survives peer review). Reply to two classmates.

Accommodations & access. The principle + summary are the required reading path; the Cipher Lab is keyboard-operable and announces results. Respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 7.04 Guarding Networks, Devices & Data
pages.html:
Unit 7 · Lesson 7.04

Guarding Networks, Devices & Data

I can…
  • analyze security & privacy risks of networks and connected devices;
  • protect computer hardware from exploitation;
  • recognize the risks of public Wi-Fi, and explain why data on the Internet is permanent.

🧭 More connections, more doors

Back in Unit 2 you mapped your network. Every device on it — laptop, phone, smart TV, doorbell, watch — is a door into your digital life. The Internet of Things multiplied those doors faster than anyone secured them: a cheap smart bulb with a default password is a real way into a home network.

Network & device privacy: the essentials

  • Change default passwords. Routers and smart devices ship with factory passwords that are published online. The single most exploited weakness in home networks.
  • Update (patch) everything. Updates fix the holes worms and attackers hunt for. "Remind me later" is an open door.
  • Segment where you can. A guest network keeps that smart bulb away from your laptop.
  • Know what your devices phone home. Connected devices constantly send data; check what a device collects before you trust it in your home.

Protecting the hardware itself

Not all exploitation is remote. Physical access to a machine is a security event, and hardware has its own defenses:

DefenseStops…
Lock screens & auto-lockAnyone using an unattended, logged-in device.
Disabling unused USB portsMalicious USB drives ("found" in a parking lot) that auto-run malware.
Managed/restricted physical accessTampering with servers, planting devices, stealing drives.
Cyber-security software (antivirus, firewall)Known malware and unauthorized network connections.

This is why the same locks/permissions logic you met at the shell (Unit 5) shows up physically: security is layered — a wall for the network, a wall for the device, a wall for the data.

Public Wi-Fi: convenient and risky

Free Wi-Fi at a café, airport, or mall is a public access point — and using it has a bargain buried in the fine print:

  • Read the terms. That "I agree" often grants the operator the right to track your activity, collect data, and show ads. Free access is rarely free of cost to your privacy.
  • Assume others can see your traffic. On an open network, an attacker nearby can attempt to intercept unencrypted data. Stick to https sites (that 🔒 = encryption from 7.03), avoid banking, and consider a VPN.
  • Beware fake hotspots. "Free_Airport_WiFi" might be an attacker's laptop. When in doubt, use your phone's own data.

The data that never dies

Here's the privacy fact that outlasts every setting: data on the Internet is effectively permanent. Once something is posted, sent, or uploaded, copies spread — screenshots, backups, caches, archives, other people's phones. "Delete" removes your copy, not the others. Your accumulated data forms an online identity and a digital footprint that future schools, employers, and strangers can find.

The permanence test: before you post or send anything, ask — am I okay with this existing forever, findable by anyone, out of my control? If not, don't. (You'll go deeper on the digital footprint and social media in Unit 8 — for now, treat every post as permanent, because it is.)

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Name one connected device in your life you've never thought about as a security risk. What data does it collect, and what's one thing you could check or change about it?

pages.title: 7.05 Standing Up Online
pages.html:
Unit 7 · Lesson 7.05

Standing Up Online

I can…
  • describe the consequences of cyberbullying — for the target and for the bully;
  • explain why inaction has consequences, and how reporting leads to positive outcomes;
  • build concrete strategies to combat cyberbullying and harassment.

🧭 Security is also about people

We've guarded data and devices. But the most important thing to protect online is people — including yourself. Cyberbullying is the use of digital tools to harass, threaten, humiliate, or exclude someone. Because it follows you home through your screen, and because a post can spread instantly and permanently (7.04), its harm can be relentless.

The consequences run both ways

For the targetFor the person doing the bullying
Anxiety, depression, isolation, falling grades, and in serious cases danger to their safety and health.School discipline, loss of friendships and reputation, and — because the evidence is permanent — a digital record that can follow them to college and jobs.
It is never the target's fault, and no one should face it alone.Serious harassment can carry legal consequences for the person responsible.
Florida law: the Jeffrey Johnson Stand Up for All Students Act. Florida requires every school district to prohibit bullying and harassment — including cyberbullying, and including acts that happen off-campus but disrupt a student's education. It also protects people who report in good faith. In short: your school is legally required to have a way for you to report this, and to act on it.

The bystander's choice: why inaction has a cost

Most people who witness cyberbullying aren't the target or the bully — they're the audience. And the audience decides what happens next. Doing nothing isn't neutral:

  • Silence signals approval. Bullying that gets likes, shares, or laughs escalates; bullying that gets no oxygen often stops.
  • The target feels the crowd. To someone being targeted, a hundred silent witnesses feel like a hundred people who agree.
  • Unreported harm continues. The same is true of any unsafe online behavior you witness — predatory messages, threats, someone in crisis. If no one who sees it reports it, it keeps happening.

Reporting works — the positive outcomes

Speaking up, safely, changes outcomes:

  • It gets the target support and can stop the harm.
  • It creates a record (screenshots, reports) that lets schools and platforms act.
  • It shifts the culture: when reporting is normal, harassment loses its audience.

Who to tell: a trusted adult — parent/guardian, teacher, counselor, coach; your school (as the Jeffrey Johnson Act requires); the platform's report button; and, for threats or danger, law enforcement. Reporting is not "tattling" — it's exactly the "report suspicious activity" instinct from the social-engineering lesson, aimed at protecting a person.

Strategies that actually help

If you're targetedIf you witness it
Don't retaliate — it escalates and muddies who's at fault.Don't amplify — no likes, shares, or "just joking" pile-ons.
Document — screenshot with dates before blocking.Support the target — a private "I saw that, you okay?" matters enormously.
Block & report — use platform tools; adjust privacy (7.02).Report — to the platform and a trusted adult.
Tell a trusted adult — you deserve backup.Speak up if safe — even one voice saying "not cool" breaks the crowd effect.

✍️ Bring it together: the Defender's Dossier

You now have everything for the unit project. Open "The Defender's Dossier": analyze a real breach, then build a public "defend yourself online" artifact — and your anti-cyberbullying strategy is a required part of it.

You're not alone. If anything in this lesson is happening to you or someone you know, please tell a trusted adult or your instructor. In the U.S. you can also reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) any time. Reaching out is strength, not weakness.

pages.html:
Unit 8 · Territory Eight · The Summit

Intelligence & the Digital Citizen: Drawing Your Own Map 🗺️

The final territory. You've charted the machine, the network, code, data, the command line, and security. Now you climb to the summit and look out over the whole landscape — asking not just how computing works, but what it's doing to us, and what kind of digital citizen you choose to be. Then you draw your own map.

Your route to the summit

  1. 8.01 — The Thinking Machine
    The history of AI, the question "can machines think?", and how machine learning already shapes your day. Play Turing's own game.
  2. 8.01b — The Generative Turn
    How today's chatbots, image makers, and coding assistants actually work — and why a tool that only predicts the next word is so often confidently wrong.
  3. 8.02 — The Expanding Frontier
    Robots, the Internet of Things, augmented and virtual reality, and machines that talk to each other without us.
  4. 8.03 — Truth, Media & Your Footprint
    Bias and misinformation, deepfakes, social media, and the permanent trail you leave behind.
  5. 8.04 — Computing, Society & Access
    How computing reshapes work and money, who gets left out, and the law and ethics of it all.
  6. 8.05 — The Healthy Digital Life
    Screen time, movement, sleep, and using technology to live well — then launch your capstone.
  7. Waypoint 8 + the course capstone: Draw Your Own Map.

What you'll be able to do

  • Explain how AI and machine learning work in the world — their promise and their limits.
  • Analyze emerging technologies and the impact of digital media on truth, culture, and yourself.
  • Reason about access, equity, law, and ethics in computing — and about your own digital well-being.
  • Synthesize the whole year into a published argument about computing and society.

The capstone: Draw Your Own Map

Draw Your Own Map is the culmination of the entire course. You'll take a real question about computing and society, argue a clear position backed by evidence, weave in what you learned across all eight territories, and publish it for a real audience — reviewed in the Council one last time. It's your proof that you can do what the course promised on day one: use computer science as a liberal art — a critical lens for reading the world.

Look how far you've come. Remember Base Camp, where you read Jeannette Wing and argued about whether computer science is a liberal art? You've now lived the answer for a year. This unit — and your capstone — is where you say what you think it all means.
Accommodations & access. Self-paced; interactives keyboard-operable and screen-reader friendly; the capstone may be an essay, slide deck, video, podcast, or illustrated site — your voice, your medium. IEP/504 supports arranged confidentially — message your instructor.

pages.title: 8.01 The Thinking Machine
pages.html:
Unit 8 · Lesson 8.01

The Thinking Machine

I can…
  • trace the history of AI and describe how we test for machine "intelligence";
  • give major real-world applications of AI and machine learning;
  • explain how predictive AI uses the past to forecast the future.

🧭 A 75-year-old question, suddenly urgent

You already met the seeds of this in Unit 4, when you trained a model in Teachable Machine and watched it learn from your data. Now zoom out. Artificial intelligence — machines performing tasks we associate with human intelligence — has gone from science fiction to something in your pocket, and it forces a question first asked seriously in 1950: can a machine think?

📜 Primary source: Turing's Imitation Game (1950)

Alan M. Turing, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." Mind, Vol. LIX, No. 236 (1950). The paper that founded the field of AI — before the word "AI" even existed.

📄 Read the paper (PDF, UMBC) →

Access: selectable-text PDF (screen-reader friendly). Required reading: Section 1 ("The Imitation Game") and skim Section 6 (his answers to objections). The key passages are quoted below.

"I propose to consider the question, 'Can machines think?'"

Turing found that question hopeless to define — so he replaced it with a game. An interrogator chats by text with a hidden human and a hidden machine, and must tell which is which. If the machine fools the interrogator as often as a human would, Turing argued, quibbling over whether it "really thinks" misses the point.

Turing's move is pure computational thinking: an unanswerable question ("can it think?") is decomposed and reframed into a testable one ("can it imitate?"). He also predicted the objections — including "Lady Lovelace's Objection" (Unit 3!), that a machine can only do what it's programmed to. His reply: a machine might still surprise its creators. Seventy-five years later, that's exactly the debate around modern AI.

🛠️ Explore: play the interrogator

Take Turing's role. Read six short exchanges and judge each responder: human or machine? Then see what fooled you — and why the test is harder than it sounds.

Open in a new tab if needed: The Imitation Game ↗

How machines "learn" — and where it already works

Most of today's AI is machine learning: instead of a programmer writing every rule, the system finds patterns in mountains of data (exactly what you did with Teachable Machine, at planetary scale). Trained well, it drives real applications:

FieldWhat AI/ML does there
MedicalSpot tumors in scans, flag drug interactions, help diagnose from symptoms and images.
SpaceSteer rovers that can't wait for Earth's commands; sift telescope data for new worlds.
AutomotiveRecognize pedestrians, lanes, and signs for driver-assist and self-driving systems.
EverydayTranslation, voice assistants, spam filters, recommendations, photo search.

Predictive AI: forecasting from the past

A powerful branch aims at the future. Predictive AI feeds historical data into a model to forecast what's likely next — the same hypothesis-and-model thinking from your Unit 4 capstone, automated and scaled:

  • Weather — tomorrow's forecast from decades of atmospheric patterns.
  • Markets — models estimating how a stock or sector may move (never perfectly).
  • Sports — win probabilities from seasons of play-by-play data.
  • Your feed — predicting the next video you'll watch to keep you watching.

And its limits are the ones you already know: predictive AI is only as good as its data, and it fails when the future stops resembling the past. A model trained on yesterday can't see a genuinely new tomorrow.

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to "Can Machines Think?" — the discussion that closes the loop Lovelace opened. Post your position (with a quoted line from Turing), then reply to two classmates, ideally across the divide.

Accommodations & access. Quoted passages + summary are the required reading path; the game is keyboard-operable and announced. Respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 8.01b The Generative Turn
pages.html:
Unit 8 · Lesson 8.01b

The Generative Turn

I can…
  • explain in plain language how a generative AI produces text, images, or code;
  • connect that machinery back to prediction and machine learning I already know;
  • name why these tools are confidently wrong — hallucination, bias, and no sense of truth;
  • use a generative tool as a scholar: to learn, to verify, and always with disclosure.

🧭 From imitation to generation

In 8.01 you played Turing's Imitation Game — a machine trying to pass as human in conversation. For seventy years that was mostly a thought experiment. Then, very recently, a new kind of AI arrived that doesn't just classify or forecast: it generates. Ask it for a sonnet, a study plan, a picture of a lighthouse, or a working function, and it writes one that never existed before. This is generative AI, and the tools you've heard of — chatbots, image generators, coding assistants — are its most visible face.

It reopens the oldest question in this course. Ada Lovelace insisted in 1843 that a machine "has no pretensions whatever to originate anything" (Unit 3). Turing replied that a machine might still surprise its creators (8.01). When a chatbot writes a poem it was never handed, whose side does that prove? Hold that question — you'll argue it in the Agora.

The trick underneath: predicting the next word

A large language model (the engine inside a text chatbot) does something startlingly simple at its core: it predicts the next chunk of text, over and over. Trained on a staggering amount of human writing, it learns the statistical shape of language — which word tends to follow which. Give it "The capital of France is," and the most probable continuation is "Paris." Give it the first line of a story, and it predicts a plausible second line, then a third, building a whole paragraph one guess at a time.

You have met this idea before. In 4.04 and 8.01, predictive AI used the past to forecast the future — tomorrow's weather, the next video in your feed. A language model is the same engine pointed at language: the "future" it forecasts is simply the next word. It's autocomplete that read most of the internet. Image and code generators work on the same principle, predicting the next pixel-pattern or the next line of code from mountains of examples.

🛠️ Explore: be the autocomplete

No login, no screen required — do this on paper or out loud, alone or with someone.

  1. Play the model. One person says three or four words of a sentence ("On Saturday mornings I like to…"). The other must instantly add one word — whatever feels most likely to come next — then hand it back. Alternate, one word at a time, until you have a few sentences.
  2. Notice what you did. You never planned the whole sentence. You predicted each next word from the pattern of the words so far. That is the entire trick of a language model — just trained on billions of sentences instead of your own memory.
  3. Break it. Now start with something you know nothing about: "The melting point of gallium is…" Add a confident-sounding number anyway. You just hallucinated — produced fluent text with no idea whether it's true. So does the machine, for exactly the same reason: it's built to sound likely, not to be right.

The point of the game is the discovery in step 3: fluency and truth are two different things, and a next-word predictor optimizes for the first.

Where it already works

Generative AI is now a major application of machine learning — the newest branch of the story you traced across the whole course, and part of why "AI, ease of use" appears on the trend line you studied in Unit 1. Trained well and used carefully, it helps people:

KindWhat it generates — and a real use
TextDrafts, summaries, translations, explanations — a tireless study partner that can rephrase a hard idea five ways.
CodeSuggests functions, explains errors, writes test cases — the coding assistant you met in our class AI policy.
Images / audioIllustrations, mock-ups, voices — from a text description alone.
LearningOn-demand tutoring for lifelong learning — ask it to quiz you, or explain recursion "like I'm twelve."

…and where it fails, by design

Your Base Camp agreement warned that AI tools are "often confidently wrong." Now you know why. Because the machine predicts likely-sounding text rather than checking facts, its weaknesses aren't bugs to be patched — they come from how it works:

  • Hallucination. It will invent facts, quotations, citations, and even court cases — stated with total confidence — because a made-up source can look every bit as "likely" as a real one.
  • Bias. It learned from human writing, so it can absorb and repeat the stereotypes and blind spots baked into that writing (the data-quality lesson from 4.04, at planetary scale).
  • No sense of truth or "now." It has no lived experience and no built-in fact-checker; its knowledge is frozen at training time unless a tool looks things up for it.
  • Fluent fakes. The same power that drafts an essay can mass-produce deepfakes, fake reviews, and propaganda — the misinformation you'll classify in 8.03, now cheap and automatic.

So the scholar's stance from Unit 0 isn't optional politeness — it's the only safe way to use the tool: treat every output as a confident draft from a stranger who never checks their facts. Verify against a trusted source, keep your own thinking in charge, and disclose when and how you used it.

Optional — catch a hallucination in the wild. If you have access to a school-approved AI chatbot, ask it for something you can check: "List three books by [an author you know well]" or "What's the population of [your town]?" Verify each claim against a trusted source and note any it got wrong or invented. Keep it to public, non-personal questions, and never paste in private or confidential information. (Following our class AI-use policy from Base Camp.)

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Take this straight into "Can Machines Think?" When a generative model writes a poem it was never given, is it originating (as Lovelace said it never could) or just doing "whatever we know how to order it to perform," at a very long distance? Bring one thing a generative tool does impressively — and one thing it got revealingly wrong — and quote a line from Turing to anchor your case. Then reply to two classmates, ideally across the divide.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

In a few sentences: explain generative AI to someone who's never used it, using the "be the autocomplete" game — and finish with the one habit you'll keep whenever you use one of these tools, and why.

Accommodations & access. The "be the autocomplete" activity is fully unplugged — no device, screen reader, or account needed; do it aloud, on paper, or by typing. The optional chatbot task can be skipped with no loss. Respond to the Logbook by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).
