pages.title: 8.02 The Expanding Frontier
pages.html:
Unit 8 · Lesson 8.02

The Expanding Frontier

I can…
  • describe how robotics addresses human challenges, and how devices talk to each other without us (M2M/IoT);
  • explain virtual and augmented reality, and emerging features of smart devices and vehicles;
  • analyze the challenges people face learning new interfaces, and how technology reshapes organizations and personal life.

🧭 Beyond the screen

Computing is leaving the desktop and spreading into the physical world — into machines that move, spaces that respond, and objects that talk to each other. You're studying this course in a VR-capable program, so you're already living on this frontier. Let's name what's out here.

Robots: computing that acts on the world

A robot is a computer with a body — sensors for input, a program to decide, and motors for output (the input→process→output loop from Unit 1, made physical). We build them to take on challenges that are dull, dirty, dangerous, or beyond human limits:

  • Dangerous: defusing bombs, inspecting reactors, search-and-rescue in collapsed buildings.
  • Precise/repetitive: surgical robots steadier than any hand; factory arms that never tire.
  • Unreachable: rovers on Mars, submersibles in the deep ocean.
  • Assistive: prosthetics, exoskeletons, and mobility aids that restore what people have lost.

When devices talk to each other: M2M & the IoT

You met the Internet of Things in security (Unit 7). Here's the deeper idea: much of the traffic on modern networks isn't people at all — it's machine-to-machine (M2M) communication, devices coordinating with no human in the loop:

  • Your smartwatch tells your phone your heart rate, which tells an app, which may alert your doctor.
  • A smart thermostat reads outdoor-weather servers and adjusts before you're cold.
  • Self-driving cars will "talk" to each other and to traffic signals to prevent collisions.

This quietly reshapes personal life: convenience and health insights on one hand; constant data collection and new dependencies on the other (which is why the privacy and security habits from Unit 7 matter more every year).

Virtual and augmented reality

Virtual Reality (VR)Augmented Reality (AR)
Replaces your world with a computer-generated one (a headset takes you elsewhere).Overlays digital things onto the real world (directions on your windshield, a creature on your street through your phone).
Uses: training simulations, virtual field trips, therapy, design walkthroughs — and your own VR seminars.Uses: surgery guidance, repair instructions in your view, live translation of signs, games.

Optional exploration: if you have a VR headset, join this unit's optional VR experience to reflect on immersion firsthand — but everything here works fully without it.

Emerging features — and the humans using them

Smart devices and vehicles keep gaining features: foldable screens, health sensors that spot atrial fibrillation, cars that update overnight and park themselves, voice and gesture control, on-device AI. But every new feature meets a human who has to learn it — and that's a real design challenge:

  • Physical challenges: tiny touch targets, gestures that strain, interfaces unusable with low vision, tremor, or limited mobility.
  • Cognitive challenges: buried menus, inconsistent icons, features with no obvious starting point, "mode confusion."

The best technology reduces these barriers instead of adding them — which is exactly the accessibility question you'll take up in 8.04. Good design is a form of respect.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Name one emerging technology from this lesson you're genuinely excited about and one that worries you. For each, give one reason. (You can pick the same one twice — that tension is the honest answer.)

pages.title: 8.03 Truth, Media & Your Footprint
pages.html:
Unit 8 · Lesson 8.03

Truth, Media & Your Footprint

I can…
  • analyze digital media for bias, and tell fact from opinion;
  • identify misinformation techniques — clickbait, misleading stats, deepfakes, propaganda;
  • explain how social media shapes culture, self-image, and my permanent digital footprint.

🧭 The most powerful media system in history — pointed at you

In Unit 2 you learned the Internet delivers everything without checking whether it's true. In Unit 7 you saw data is permanent. Now combine those with AI (8.01) and social media, and you get the defining challenge of digital citizenship: a flood of media, some true, some engineered to deceive, all competing for your attention — and shaping who you become.

Bias, and fact vs. opinion

All media carries bias — a perspective shaped by who made it and why. Bias isn't automatically bad (everyone has a viewpoint), but you must detect it to weigh a source. The first tool is separating two things people constantly blur:

FactOpinion
Can be checked and verified. "The bill passed 60–40."A judgment or preference. "The bill is a disaster."
True or false regardless of who says it.Valid to hold — but not evidence by itself.

Watch for opinions wearing fact's clothing: "objectively," "everyone knows," "the truth is…" Those phrases often signal a viewpoint hoping you won't check.

🛠️ Explore: spot the manipulation

Misinformation is media crafted to distort, exaggerate, or misrepresent. Train your radar on eight specimens — clickbait, misleading statistics, deepfakes/fabrication, opinion-as-fact, and propaganda — plus honest reporting you should not flag.

Open in a new tab if needed: Spot the Manipulation ↗

Deepfakes deserve special note: AI (8.01) can now fabricate photo-realistic video and cloned voices of real people saying things they never said. The consequences of spreading misinformation are real — slander, libel, and defamation are legal harms, and a fabricated clip can damage a person or a democracy before the truth catches up. Your defense is the one from Unit 2: slow down, check the source, read laterally, and don't share until you've verified.

Social media: a short history, a long shadow

Social media began (mid-2000s) as a way to stay connected — profiles, friends, photos. In under two decades it became the main way billions get news, form opinions, run businesses, and see themselves. That's enormous power, and it cuts both ways:

  • Culture: it can spread movements, art, and knowledge globally in hours — and also outrage, trends, and misinformation just as fast.
  • Persona & self-image: curated "highlight reels" set impossible comparisons; algorithms reward whatever keeps you scrolling, not whatever's good for you. Knowing this is the first defense.

Your digital footprint is permanent

Every post, like, comment, and account builds your digital footprint — the trail of you online. Recall Unit 7: data is effectively permanent, and "delete" rarely means gone. Colleges, employers, and strangers can and do look. Your footprint is a kind of reputation you're writing in ink, in public, for years.

Two habits of a good digital citizen: (1) Curate what you create — post as if a future you, and anyone who matters to you, will read it, because they can. (2) Verify before you amplify — every share is a small act of publishing; don't lend your footprint to a lie.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Search your own name (and common handles). What's findable? Is it the footprint you'd want a future employer — or a future you — to see? Name one thing you'd add, remove, or change.

pages.title: 8.04 Computing, Society & Access
pages.html:
Unit 8 · Lesson 8.04

Computing, Society & Access

I can…
  • describe how computing reshapes business, commerce, and access to information;
  • analyze the digital divide and how technology can improve accessibility for people with disabilities;
  • distinguish the legal from the ethical use of technology and media.

🧭 Computing rewired the economy

Every business you interact with runs on computing. It didn't just speed up old ways of working — it created entirely new ones:

  • E-commerce & global reach: a one-person shop can sell worldwide; a warehouse an ocean away ships to your door tomorrow.
  • New models: streaming replaced ownership; apps connect riders to drivers and freelancers to clients; data itself became a product.
  • Whole job categories appeared (app developer, data analyst, cloud engineer, content creator) while others shrank — the careers thread from Unit 1, playing out economy-wide.

Information is power — and it isn't evenly shared

Access to information has huge economic and societal consequences. Whoever can find, afford, and use information can start businesses, learn skills, access services, and participate in democracy. Whoever can't, falls behind. That gap has a name:

The digital divide — the gap between those with reliable access to computing and the Internet and those without. It runs between wealthy and poor neighborhoods, cities and rural areas, and rich and developing nations. A student with fast home internet, a device, and digital skills has advantages compounding daily over one without — in school, work, and life.

Possible bridges (you'll weigh these): public libraries and school device programs, community broadband, low-cost hardware, offline-capable tools, and digital-literacy education (like this course). Access is not just a tech problem — it's a justice problem with tech solutions.

Technology as an equalizer: accessibility

Computing can also widen access — especially for people with disabilities. When technology is designed well (recall the interface challenges in 8.02), it removes barriers that the physical world imposes:

Assistive technologyOpens access for…
Screen readers & text-to-speechPeople who are blind or have low vision.
Captions & transcriptsPeople who are deaf or hard of hearing.
Speech-to-text, switch & eye-gaze controlPeople with limited mobility.
Adjustable text, contrast & reading toolsPeople with dyslexia, ADHD, or low vision.

This is why every widget and page in this course is keyboard-operable, screen-reader labeled, and high-contrast — the accessibility standards you've seen in every "Accommodations & access" box are this benchmark, lived. Accessible design helps everyone (captions in a loud room; voice control while cooking) — good access is good design.

Legal vs. ethical: two different questions

In Unit 6 you licensed your team's tool and met the ACM Code. Here's the distinction sharpened. Technology use raises legal ramifications — real laws with real consequences:

  • Copyright & licensing (Unit 6), privacy laws, anti-harassment law (the Jeffrey Johnson Act, Unit 7), defamation (slander/libel, 8.03), computer-fraud and hacking statutes.
  • Legal use of communication media & devices: respecting others' rights, following platform terms and school/state policy, and knowing that laws change and vary by place — staying current is part of responsible use.
Legal ≠ ethical. Something can be perfectly legal and still wrong (harvesting a friend's public data to manipulate them; a design that's addictive by intent), and occasionally something feels ethical but breaks a law. A digital citizen asks both questions: "Is this allowed?" and "Is this right?" The law is the floor; ethics is the aspiration.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Describe one way computing has widened access for someone (maybe you), and one way the digital divide has held someone back. What's one realistic action a school, company, or government could take to narrow the gap?

pages.title: 8.05 The Healthy Digital Life
pages.html:
Unit 8 · Lesson 8.05

The Healthy Digital Life

I can…
  • make choices about screen time that protect my mental and physical well-being;
  • explain the links between device use and sedentary behavior, sleep, and eye strain;
  • assess how digital health trackers can help — and their limits.

🧭 The user is also a body

A whole year on how computing works — and the last lesson is about you, the human at the keyboard. The same devices that connect and empower you also affect your sleep, posture, eyes, and mind. A digital citizen manages that relationship on purpose, rather than letting an algorithm manage it for them.

Four honest trade-offs

IssueWhat the evidence suggestsA practical habit
Screen time & mindHeavy, passive, or late-night use is linked to worse mood, focus, and sleep — quality and timing matter as much as hours.Set intentional limits; protect the hour before sleep; choose active use over endless scrolling.
Sedentary behaviorDevice use often means sitting for long stretches, correlated with real physical-health risks.Move every 30–60 min; take calls walking; stand to read.
Eye strain & blue lightLong screen sessions cause blurred vision, headaches, and eye fatigue; evening blue light can disrupt sleep.20-20-20 rule (every 20 min, look 20 ft away for 20 s); night mode after dark; blink and adjust brightness.
Health trackersWearables can nudge healthy behavior (steps, sleep, activity reminders) and flag issues — but can also cause anxiety, and they collect sensitive data.Use the nudges you find motivating; check what data is shared (Unit 7!); don't mistake a number for your health.

These are trade-offs, not commandments. Technology isn't the enemy — unexamined use is. The goal is to be the one making the choice.

✍️ Do this: the Well-Being Check

Open the assignment "Well-Being Check." You'll track your own device use for a few days, analyze the data (a small taste of Unit 4's data skills, turned on yourself), and design one realistic change — then predict its effect like a hypothesis.

🗺️ The Summit: Draw Your Own Map

You've reached the top. It's time for the capstone that closes the course.

On day one, Jeannette Wing asked whether computer science is a liberal art — a lens for reading the world. For a year you've built that lens: the machine, the network, code, algorithms and data, the command line, software craft, security, and now intelligence and society. Draw Your Own Map is where you use it.

Open the "Draw Your Own Map" capstone: choose a real question about computing and society, take a clear position, back it with evidence, weave in what you learned across the eight territories, and publish it for a real audience — with one final pass through the Council. It is your answer, in your voice, to the question this course has been asking all along: what does computing mean, and what kind of digital citizen will you be?

Then, one last Logbook entry. Reopen your very first Base Camp reflection — what you thought "computer science" meant before this course. Read it. Then write what you think now. That's the map you drew.
Accommodations & access. The Well-Being Check can use device screen-time reports, a paper tally, or estimates — no tracker required. The capstone may be an essay, deck, video, podcast, or site. Sensitive-topic and extended options per IEP/504 (confidential).

Finish the summit — and the course: complete Draw Your Own Map and Waypoint 8. Then look back at how far you've come, explorer. 🦉

At the shell, the filesystem is text you type paths into. Build it as a place you can walk through. In your own Arthur space, construct the filesystem as a walkable tree:

  1. Root at the top/center, then at least three nested directories built as containers, platforms, or rooms-inside-rooms so the hierarchy is obvious.
  2. Files as named objects placed inside the right directories.
  3. Draw the absolute path from root to one deep file (e.g., /home/explorer/logs/day1.txt) as a highlighted trail you can follow.
  4. The vault. Mark one directory as the permission-locked vault and show what "locked" means — who may enter, who is refused.

assignments.title: Script Lab Log
assignments.html:
Submit a screenshot + short text, or a recorded walkthrough.

Prove your five challenges — and that you can read your own scripts.

  1. Complete all 5 Script Lab challenges (lessons 6.01–6.02) in one sitting. Screenshot the 🏆 all-complete state.
  2. Annotate your Countdown script (challenge 5), line by line. For each line: what it does, in your own words. Two lines deserve special care: the while [ $N -gt 0 ] line — what question is being asked, and in Unit 3's language, what kind of structure is this? And the N=$((N - 1)) line — what would happen if you deleted it, and how does the Lab protect you when that goes wrong?
  3. Translate (2–3 sentences). Write the Gatekeeper challenge (age check) as Unit 3 JavaScript pseudocode. What changed? What didn't?

assignments.title: The Toolmaker's Guild (Unit 6 Team Project)
assignments.html:
Team project (2–3, async; solo track available — ask your instructor). Deliverables live in your team thread + the class showcase; submit links here.

Guilds built cathedrals; yours builds a tool — through the full professional cycle: plan → build → review → revise → license → publish. All collaboration is asynchronous: your team thread is your workshop.

Phase 1 — Charter & design (after lesson 6.03): choose a tool idea in your team thread (argue trade-offs: cost/features/usability), then write the design doc together: requirements · structural design (decomposed chunks with owners) · test plan (incl. one break-it input) · time estimates. The doc must exist before code does — that ordering is graded.

Phase 2 — Build & Council (with lesson 6.04): build to the plan in the Script Lab. The tool must include: input via read, a validation loop, selection, iteration, honest names, a header comment naming the team and who built what, and why-comments at decisions. Keep a dated contribution log in the thread (reviews and testing count as contributions). Then sit the Council (separate assignment) and revise from the reviews received, logging what changed and why — or why not.

Phase 3 — License, publish, retrospect (after lesson 6.05): choose a license (open source MIT-style or GPL-style, freeware-style, or all-rights-reserved) + one paragraph defending the choice; credit every source you drew on (AI assists disclosed per our class agreement); publish the final script + design doc + a 3–5 sentence user's guide to the class showcase — written for someone who has never seen your team thread. Finally, each member posts an individual retrospective (~150 words or recorded): compare this team build to your solo Unit 3 project — what did collaboration change about the design? Biggest strength and biggest friction of the collaborative process, with one concrete example of each?

Accommodations: fully asynchronous; roles flexible (reviewer/tester/documenter are contributions); retrospective typed or recorded; extended timelines per IEP/504 (confidential).

assignments.title: The Council: Review Round
assignments.html:
Structured async peer review. You are graded on the reviews you give — making others' work better is the work.

Part A — Give two reviews. You'll be assigned two other teams' tools (script + design doc). For each, review with all four lenses from lesson 6.04:

  1. Functionality — run it (Script Lab). Does it do what its design doc promises? Try their break-it input and one of your own.
  2. Readability — could a stranger follow the code? Point to one honest name or good comment, and one spot that confused you (quote the line).
  3. Usability — clear prompts? Survives bad input? Output a human can use?
  4. Style & standards — header comment present? Names consistent? Matches their stated conventions?

Format per review: at least one specific strength (quote it) + at least two specific, actionable suggestions (line + what to change + why) + one sentence on whether the code kept the design doc's promises. Kind, specific, about the code — never the coder.

Part B — Respond to the reviews you received (in your team thread): address every point — fixed (what changed) or declined (why not). Silence isn't an option; disagreement with reasons is.

Part C — Reviewer's reflection (2–3 sentences): what did reviewing someone else's code teach you about your own? Name one thing you changed because of something you saw in a peer's tool.

"Looks good!" reviews score Emerging regardless of how good the tool is.

Accommodations: reviews and responses typed or recorded; the four-lens list is your checklist; no time limits. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

assignments.title: VR Build — The Blueprint Room

assignments.title: The Defender's Dossier (Unit 7 Project)
assignments.html:
A two-part dossier: a breach analysis (written or recorded) + a public "defend yourself online" artifact (guide, poster, slides, or video). Submit link(s) here.

Part 1 — Breach Analysis. Choose a real, documented cyber attack or data breach from the last ~10 years (from your instructor's vetted list). Using reputable, cited sources (2+, via a citation tool), answer:

  1. What happened? In your own words: what was attacked, and how did the attackers get in (social engineering? malware — virus or worm? stolen credentials? unpatched system?)?
  2. Who was hurt, and how? Evaluate the social impact (whose data, and what could be done with it) and the economic impact (ransom, downtime, fines, lost trust).
  3. What would have stopped it? Point to specific defenses from this unit (patching, verification against social engineering, encryption/key management, permissions, MFA). Name the one that mattered most, and why.

Part 2 — Defend Yourself Online. Create a public-facing artifact for a real audience you choose (younger students, family, teammates), including: 3–5 concrete protection habits from this unit (privacy settings, app permissions, strong/unique passwords + MFA, spotting social engineering, public-Wi-Fi caution, the permanence test); and an anti-cyberbullying section — what to do if you're targeted, what to do if you witness it, and how/where to report (noting reporting leads to positive outcomes and that help exists).

Accommodations: no time limit; artifact medium is your choice (writing, design, slides, recording); analysis typed or recorded. Sensitive-topic alternatives per IEP/504 (confidential).

assignments.title: VR Build — The Citadel (Defense in Depth)
assignments.html:
VR Build · Arthur · Build it yourself
The Citadel: Defense in Depth 🛡
There's no room or experience waiting for you — you build the fortress yourself in an empty Arthur space.
How to turn it in — your choice. Either (A) a few in-headset screenshots + a short written reflection, or (B) a short recorded video walkthrough. Both earn equal credit.

This unit is about guarding something valuable — and real security is layers, not a single wall. In your own Arthur space, build a "defense in depth" citadel protecting a valuable data treasure at the center. Build concentric layers, each labeled with the control it is and the threat it stops:

  1. Outer wall — network security (firewall / secure network & device settings): stops outside intrusion.
  2. The gate — authentication (strong, unique passwords / MFA): stops unauthorized entry.
  3. The inner vault — encryption: even if someone gets in, the treasure is unreadable without the key. Show the idea that the enemy may know the system — safety rests on the key, not on hiding the method.
  4. The human weak point — social engineering. Mark one spot where an attacker bypasses every wall by fooling a person (phishing, pretexting), and note which stage of the con it is.

In your submission, play attacker for a moment: describe how someone might try each layer, and how your defense answers it. This is about protecting, never attacking — keep examples generic.

assignments.title: Well-Being Check
assignments.html:
Submit a data table + short analysis (typed or recorded). Turn Unit 4's data skills on yourself — kindly and honestly.

  1. Collect (3+ days). Track your device use with your phone's screen-time report, a wearable, or a paper tally. Record daily: total screen time, roughly how much was active (creating/learning/connecting) vs. passive (endless scrolling), and one well-being signal you can observe (sleep, energy, mood, eye strain, or time moving).
  2. Analyze. Put it in a small table. What patterns do you notice? Any relationship between passive/late-night use and your sleep, mood, or activity? An honest "no clear pattern" is a valid finding.
  3. Design one change + predict. Choose one realistic habit from lesson 8.05 and state it as a hypothesis: "If I ___, I predict ___ because ___."
  4. Reflect (2–3 sentences). Health trackers can help and can mislead or overcollect data. Would you use one here? One benefit, one concern (privacy from Unit 7 counts).

assignments.title: Draw Your Own Map (COURSE CAPSTONE)
assignments.html:
The artifact that closes the course. Publish it (essay, slide deck, video, podcast, or illustrated site), review two peers in the Council, and submit your link + final reflection here.

1. Choose your question. A real, arguable question about computing and society you care about — e.g., limits on AI in schools/hiring/policing; is social media net positive for our generation; whose job is it to close the digital divide; should deepfakes be illegal; do we own our data; is convenience-for-privacy worth it in the IoT age. (Or propose your own.)

2. Take a position and defend it with evidence: a clear thesis; 3+ reputable, cited sources (use a citation tool; evaluate them with your media-literacy skills); at least two concepts from across the course (how networks work, how AI/ML learns and fails, encryption/privacy, licenses/ethics, the digital footprint) — show you understand the technology under the issue; and a fair treatment of the strongest counter-argument.

3. Publish for a real audience (peers, younger students, families, decision-makers) in your chosen medium, to the class showcase.

4. Council review + revision: review two classmates' maps (thesis clear? evidence sound & cited? technology accurate? counter-argument fair?), then revise yours from the feedback and note what changed.

5. Final reflection — "The map I drew": reopen your Base Camp (Unit 0) reflection on what you thought computer science meant. In ~200 words (or recorded): what do you think now? How did your view change, and which unit shifted it most? End by answering, in your own words — is computer science a liberal art?

Accommodations: no time limit; medium and audience are your choice; Council review and reflection typed or recorded; extended timelines and alternative formats per IEP/504 (confidential).

quizzes.title: Waypoint 5 — Command of the Machine Check

questions.text: A shell is best described as:

answers.text: A piece of hardware inside the computer
A program that interprets your typed commands and asks the operating system to carry them out
The same thing as the Internet

questions.text: A systems administrator needs to rename 500 files on a server in another country, over a slow connection. The better interface is:

answers.text: A graphical file manager, dragging each file
The command line — one repeatable command, tiny bandwidth

questions.text: Which command answers 'where am I right now?'

answers.text: An absolute path — the full route from the root

What's the difference between > and >> when sending output to a file?

answers.text: > overwrites the file's contents; >> appends to the end

answers.text: It goes to a trash can you can restore from
It's gone — the shell has no undo and assumes you meant it

questions.text: You suspect one of 200 log files contains the word 'breach'. The professional move is:

answers.text: grep breach * — search every file in one command

answers.text: Sends grep's output lines into wc as input, so wc counts the matches
Saves the output to a file

answers.text: Each program does one thing well, and programs combine through pipes

Someone nearby watches your screen or reads your password as you type

questions.text: When evaluating the impact of a real cyber attack, you should weigh: (select all that apply)

discussions.title: Do One Thing Well
discussions.html:
In 1974, two researchers described an operating system whose bet was simplicity: many small tools, each doing one thing well, connected by pipes so their powers combine. Their design still runs most of the world's computers.

Post (~150 words): Quote one line from the paper (lesson 5.01 has the key excerpts). Then take a side: is "small pieces, freely combined" really better than "one big tool that does everything"? Defend your answer with one example from outside computing (LEGO vs. a molded toy, a kitchen of knives vs. a do-everything gadget, an orchestra vs. a one-man band…) — and name one situation where the big all-in-one tool honestly wins.

Reply to two classmates. Test their analogy: where does it hold up, where does it break?

Norms: cite your evidence, use a respectful scholarly voice, and respond — don't just post. You may type or record.

discussions.title: The Public Good
discussions.html:
The ACM Code of Ethics says computing professionals must "ensure that the public good is the central concern" (3.1) — yet no law enforces it. It's a promise a profession makes.

Post (~150 words): Quote one principle from the Code (lesson 6.05 has the key excerpts) and connect it to a real decision your Guild team just made (your tool's license, its input guards, who it serves, how you credited sources — anything). Then: the Code is ethics, a license is law you wrote. Where do they overlap in your project — and can you imagine a case where following the license would still break the Code?

Reply to two classmates. Test their example: does the principle they quoted really cover it?

Norms: cite your evidence, use a respectful scholarly voice, and respond — don't just post. You may type or record.

discussions.title: Spot the Con
discussions.html:
Attacks on people follow a predictable cycle: information gathering → relationship building → exploitation → execution.

Post (~150 words): Share a real or realistic social-engineering attempt — a phishing text, a "you've won!" DM, a fake tech-support call, a too-good giveaway. Then analyze it: which stage of the cycle is it in? What's the red flag that gives it away? What information did the attacker already have or want, and what could shrink that? (Keep examples generic — don't name real classmates.)

Reply to two classmates: name the single verification step that would defeat their example, and whether the attacker was after access, information, or money.

Norms: respectful scholarly voice; respond, don't just post. Type or record.

discussions.title: The Enemy Knows the System
discussions.html:
In 1883, Kerckhoffs insisted a cryptosystem must stay secure even if the enemy knows exactly how it works — with only the key kept secret. Claude Shannon later put it bluntly: "the enemy knows the system."

Post (~150 words): Quote the principle (lesson 7.03). Why would security experts deliberately publish their encryption algorithms for the whole world — including attackers — to study and try to break? Give one analogy from outside computing where openness makes something more trustworthy, not less (a lock rated by breaking attempts, a scientific result that survives peer review, a bridge whose engineering is public…). Then connect it to the Cipher Lab: why didn't knowing "it's a Caesar cipher" let you read the message instantly?

Reply to two classmates: test their analogy — does openness really strengthen it, or is there a hidden "key" doing the real work?

Norms: cite your evidence; respond, don't just post. Type or record.

discussions.title: Can Machines Think?
discussions.html:
This is the discussion the whole course has been building toward. In 1843 Ada Lovelace said a machine "has no pretensions whatever to originate anything." In 1950 Alan Turing replaced "Can machines think?" with a game: if a machine can imitate a human well enough to fool an interrogator, does the rest matter?

Post (~175 words): Quote one line from Turing (lesson 8.01). Then take a position: after playing the Imitation Game and living a year of this course, do you think today's AI "thinks," merely "imitates," or is that distinction even the right question? Use at least one concrete example (something an AI does well, and something it gets revealingly wrong). Then connect it back: was Lovelace right, was Turing right, or are they arguing past each other?

Reply to two classmates, ideally ones who took a different side. Push their reasoning with a genuine question — not just agreement.

Norms: cite your evidence; respectful scholarly voice; respond, don't just post. Type or record.
